segments: Directory layout: SSH consists of two independent sides
OpenSSH acts as both client (ssh) and server (sshd). Different programs in the same suite read their own configurations:
Four kinds of authentication material, four separate roles
In a typical public-key-authenticated connection, four kinds of material can be distinguished. authorized_keys and known_hosts are list files, not individual keys:
known_hosts (trust records such as peer host public keys or CAs)

The ownership exception: authorized_keys authorized_keys lives in ~/.ssh/, but it is used for inbound connections. It lists whom the server allows in, with a separate list for each user. It is fundamentally configuration read by sshd, placed in each user’s home directory for convenient self-management.

Public keys are not registered automatically The client verifies the server’s host key. With public-key authentication, the server verifies a signature made with the user’s private key. An administrator must first add the user’s public key to the target account’s authorized_keys (or use certificates or another authorization mechanism); connecting does not automatically add the visiting user’s public key to the authorization list. The client records the server’s public key only after accepting it or establishing trust in advance. Users can also authenticate with passwords or other methods, so not every connection uses a user public key.
Mutual authentication: why host keys are needed
An SSH connection does more than verify who you are; verification works in both directions:

The host key handles direction 2: it is your machine’s identity document, proving its identity back to the other side. This is what “both parties verify each other’s identity” means in the A/B machine example above.
Why verify the other direction? To prevent a man-in-the-middle attack:

An attacker connects to you, then impersonates you to accept a connection from desktop. Credentials entered by desktop go to the attacker. This is what the host key guards against: desktop records your fingerprint on the first connection and checks that it still matches on every subsequent connection.
The purpose and limits of TOFU
First connection: verify and accept the peer’s host key, then record the host public key in known_hosts
Every subsequent connection: check that the fingerprint still matches
What it cannot establish (authenticity on first use):

TOFU’s blind spot TOFU can only establish whether later connections are to the same party as the first one. It cannot establish that the first party was genuine. If you connected to an impostor the first time, checking the fingerprint offers no protection against that impostor.
Check officially published fingerprints: GitHub and cloud providers publish host key fingerprints on their official sites; compare them with ssh-keygen -lf after connecting
SSH certificates (SSH CA): large organizations issue certificates to each server and preinstall the CA public key on clients, allowing verification even on the first connection

Private networks/direct connections: these can reduce exposure, but being on the same LAN does not by itself prove identity. Ideally, obtain the fingerprint from the server console or another trusted channel and compare it

TOFU suits situations where the risk of initial trust is acceptable. Published fingerprints, a trusted console, or preconfigured trust material can strengthen the first verification. Do not disable host key checking globally just to remove the prompts.
GitHub’s git entry point and account identification

When connecting to GitHub, User git is a shared entry-point name, not your GitHub account name. GitHub identifies accounts by public key, not by username. Multiple accounts are distinguished by using the same git user with different IdentityFile values:

Directory ownership fundamentally answers “Who owns this configuration?” /etc/ssh/ belongs to the system (machine identity, managed by root); ~/.ssh/ belongs to the user (your identity, managed by you). authorized_keys sits between them: it implements server authorization but is divided into each user’s guest list, so it lives in ~/.ssh/ while serving inbound connections.
